newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Zagat surveys go international--but no Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Zagat surveys go international--but no Tokyo.

text.p: The man who eats out 10 times a week is on a diet and clearly is not going to order much as he and his wife enter their local "classy, civilised and priced accordingly" Central Park South restaurant -- you know, the one with "a private club atmosphere."

But regardless of their intentions to consume or not, Tim Zagat and his wife Nina are given "the table by the window" and staff, who are "anxious to serve," hover around them. Fellow diners join in giving the couple royal treatment, including one who comes over and whispers conspiratorily in Zagat's ear, "Try the truffles."

A city that sometimes perversely prides itself on raising inhospitality to new heights of incivility bends the rules for the Zagats, who created the little red book of the consumption revolution, the "Zagat Survey of New York Restaurants."

What started as a hobby in the early 1980s -- two food enthusiasts handing out forms for other serious eaters to fill in and rate the city's restaurants -- has turned into a book that "out-sells the Bible and the dictionary" in the Big Apple and an empire of similar where-to-eat guides criss-crossing the United States.
As his waist contracts, Tim Zagat's empire expands.
FIRST LONDON, THEN THE WORLD

Last month, the Zagats went international, publishing a guide to London restaurants based on surveys filled out by 1,700 Londoners of their favourite places. It is stuffed with the sort of catch-phrases that pepper all Zagat guides.

"Nursery food served by nanny waitresses" is a comment about Wilton's, a pricey place near St. James's park, and "irresistibly cheap" is the dubious distinction won by Fatboy's Cafe, frequented by a "raucous" Chiswick crowd.

As he ignores a waiter's recommendation of pasta to order "grilled fish and vegetables," Tim Zagat declares that London is just the first stop internationally. "We are planning a Paris guide and a Hong Kong guide, but not Tokyo," he said, sipping a glass of "plain, no frills" mineral water.

"We were thinking about Japan but the best restaurants there are private clubs. You just can't get into them without a club member. Also the Japanese frown on criticism. We are afraid that the survey group won't be straightforward, they wouldn't criticise," he said.
But he added, "Hong Kong is different. People there are willing to criticise food. We are going to do Hong Kong."
The key to the success of the Zagats' surveys is democracy. What you read is what thousands of people think of a restaurant, not what a single critic whose taste might not be yours thinks.
"SPOOKS IN TRENCHCOATS"

The Zagat surveyers have been depicted as "spooks in trenchcoats" and they include all sorts of people who love to eat out almost as often as the Zagats do. "We have CEOs filling out the forms, politicians, all sorts of people contributing. We don't pay them because we would be out of business if we did," Zagat said.

What the Zagats do pay big for is data processing to collate and condense the survey comments. From the results, they can determine what men want versus what women want, what 50-year-olds want versus what 20-year-olds want -- as least as far as food goes.
"A man thinks a big hearty meal is romantic while a woman thinks of candlelight and lilting piano music. We do breakouts of restaurants by sex, age and occasion," Zagat said.

For years, Nina Zagat said, the couple looked for great places where children could spill things. Thanks to their guide they found plenty, but now that their children have grown up they no longer need them.

The Zagats said they chose London for their first foreign guide because the quality of food in the British capital has improved dramatically and Britons are suddenly serious about food. They said the guide has been well received there but they are not surprised.

"We've gotten to the point where people want us. The mayor of Toronto literally asked us to do a book about the city because he wanted to put the city on the culinary map. The mayor of Kansas City gave us a breakfast when we came to town," Tim Zagat said.

"Restauranteurs welcome us becuse our reviews tell them what the people who eat there think about their food, decor and service. The test of any guide is accuracy and fairness and restaurants are grateful for that."
And with that, Zagat finished his fish and departed, seemingly proud that a man who made "Read It to Eat" a profitable slogan had kept to his diet.
